title: Charge
subtitle: Design a clear commitment, a reachable escape, and a useful recovery.
summary: The boss aims, locks its direction, and charges forward. It cannot turn after the lock.
learning: Tune tracking, the lock cue, the danger lane, and recovery.

demo.title: Test the attack
phaseDescriptions: Set how long the boss tracks the player. Make this phase visible.
Show the exact moment tracking stops with a clear cue.
Keep the hitbox inside the shown lane. Test it against normal movement.
Leave enough time for the player to return to range and attack.
demo.reducedMotion: Animation starts paused. Use the phase buttons or timeline to explore without playback.
demo.diagramDescription: A test diagram for a charge attack. The side path clears the danger lane; the straight path stays inside it.

steps.title: When does tracking stop?
steps.body: Choose a fixed moment. Mark it with a pose, sound, or effect.

steps.title: Can the lane be cleared?
steps.body: Compare lane width, player speed, and the time between lock and impact.

steps.title: Is recovery useful?
steps.body: Include the time needed to return to range and complete an attack.

mistakes.title: Unclear lock
mistakes.body: If tracking and lock look the same, hits feel arbitrary.

mistakes.title: Fake opening
mistakes.body: If recovery ends before the player can reach the boss, the promised opening is not real.

designNotes.title: Start with normal movement
designNotes.body: Make the basic escape work without a special ability unless that ability is the lesson.

designNotes.title: Match collision and visuals
designNotes.body: The visible danger lane must match the real hitbox.

designNotes.title: Retest after upgrades
designNotes.body: Movement, range, damage, and invulnerability can change how the attack works.

story.title: Use a clear arena
story.body: A long, open lane makes the attack easy to read. Avoid obstacles that hide the boss or the escape route.

adaptation.title: Respect player upgrades
adaptation.body: Test the attack against the abilities already available to the player. If the boss blocks an attack, show it clearly and keep another response useful.

distinction.title: Charge ≠ dash ≠ lunge
distinction.body: A charge threatens a full lane. A dash changes position. A lunge is a short attack. This page shows one kind of charge.

examples.body: A short tell leads into a straight charge that stops at terrain. Obstacles and lane width define the attack.
Its second phase chains fast charges from different angles. Shorter gaps turn one readable move into sustained pressure.
A brief lean-back signals a horizontal dash. The small arena and high damage demand a very clear cue.
Long runs, wide turns, and walls make momentum part of the encounter. The charge stays readable even when its path curves.
The lowered head announces a long rush. Body size and the open arena make distance and lateral clearance easy to read.
Brief tracking leads into a long arena-crossing charge. A circular room and 3D camera make the safe side harder to judge.

quiz.question: Normal movement cannot clear the lane after lock. What should the designer check first?
options: Reduce the time between lock and impact.
Compare lane width, player speed, and lock timing.
quiz.explanation: These three values determine whether the intended escape is possible. Test them from every expected starting position.
